query: For an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy in its uniform, fine lamellar state, whose strength and plasticity remain below industrial application requirements, what single intervention could improve performance for fasteners exposed to extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosive conditions? State the proposed intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome relative to the starting alloy, applicable operating and test boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit falsification criteria.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount (approximately 0.5 atomic percent) of Hf to the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will induce the precipitation of Hf-rich phases along the lamellar interfaces to impede grain boundary sliding and dislocation movement. This intervention will improve the alloy's strength, ductility, and creep resistance under industrial operating conditions that include extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, and corrosive environments.
generation.material_initial_state: Uniform, fine lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with mechanical properties (strength and plasticity) below industrial application requirements.
generation.intervention: Microalloying the alloy with approximately 0.5 at% Hf to promote the formation of Hf-rich precipitates at and within the interfaces of the alloy's lamellar structure.
generation.conditions: The alloy will be subjected to extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loads (including room-temperature creep), and corrosive conditions such as exposure to chloride-containing sulfuric acid solutions, similar to those encountered by fasteners in service.
generation.structural_mediator: Hf-rich precipitates that form at the lamellar interfaces act as barriers to dislocation movement and grain-boundary sliding.
generation.mechanism: The precipitated Hf-rich phase is expected to hinder the mobility of dislocations and reduce grain-boundary sliding, thereby enhancing tensile strength and ductility. Additionally, by stabilizing the interfaces, the Hf may also help in maintaining a more uniform and robust passive film, potentially mitigating the corrosion issues observed in the base alloy under aggressive conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the original alloy, the Hf-modified alloy will exhibit a notable increase in yield strength, tensile strength, and ductility, along with enhanced resistance to room-temperature creep and improved performance under corrosive attack.
generation.baseline: The unmodified AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy shows limited strength and plasticity, with lamellar interface weaknesses that contribute to cracking under mechanical and corrosive stresses.
generation.boundary: The improvements are expected to be effective within the temperature ranges and corrosive conditions typical for fastener applications. However, the extent of improved performance may be limited if temperatures or corrosive conditions exceed those tested in standard industrial scenarios.
generation.uncertainty: Although the addition of Hf has been shown to enhance high-temperature strength and ductility in similar dual-phase high-entropy alloys (PMC10647333::page::001), its effects on room-temperature creep resistance and corrosion behavior specifically in the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy remain less directly evidenced. Further, the optimum Hf concentration may require additional tuning under service-specific conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 samples: one set with a 0.5 at% Hf addition and one set as the control without Hf. Subject both sets to (a) cyclic temperature fluctuation tests covering the range of service temperatures, (b) long-term creep testing at ambient temperatures, and (c) corrosion testing in a chloride-containing sulfuric acid environment. Monitor the mechanical properties and corrosion performance over time.
measurements: Tensile tests to measure yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and plasticity
Creep tests at room temperature to quantify creep rate under constant load
Electrochemical corrosion tests (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization) to evaluate passive film stability and pitting resistance
Microstructural analyses (using SEM/TEM) to confirm the formation and distribution of Hf-rich precipitates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Hf-modified alloy does not show statistically significant improvements in yield strength, tensile strength, ductility, creep resistance, and corrosion resistance compared to the unmodified alloy under the specified experimental conditions, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

## Abstract
Dual-phase high-entropy alloys with excellent room temperature and high-temperature properties have been widely studied as potential high-temperature structural materials. However, interface weakening causes its high-temperature performance to decline at higher temperatures, severely limiting further development. In this study, a series of Al17Cr10Fe36Ni36Mo1Hfx (x = 0, 0.03, 0.15, 0.3, 0.5, and 0.8 at%) alloys were prepared to study the effect of Hf content on the microstructure and mechanical properties of the matrix alloy. The results indicate that with the addition of the Hf, the Hf-rich phase began to precipitate at the interface and inside the B2 phase in the matrix alloy. In contrast, the morphology of both the FCC and B2 phases had no noticeable change. With the increase in Hf content, the high-temperature strength and ductility of the alloy first increased and then decreased, while the room temperature performance remained almost unchanged. ## Abstract
In this work, the influence of temperature on the corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy in a chloride-containing sulfuric acid solution was investigated using electrochemical measurement, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, and scanning electron microscopy. Results show that the passive film of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 is stable in chloride-containing sulfuric acid solutions at low temperatures, while an unstable film forms on the alloy at high temperatures. Furthermore, temperature changes the proportion of hydroxide and oxide in Fe and Cr, but it has no noticeable effect on Al and Ni, which is a significant factor on the passive behavior. L12 phase exhibits good corrosion resistance at different temperatures. Pitting occurred on B2 phase in the chloride-containing sulfuric acid solution at a low temperature of 5 °C, while pitting and dissolution take place on AlCoCrFeNi2.1 in the acid solution at room temperature and above.
